learn.hook: A wink, a postcard, a voice note and a namaste: four very different ways to say something!
points: The lesson 'Carrier of Words' is about communication, that is, how messages travel from one person to another.
Verbal communication uses words, spoken or written. Non-verbal communication uses gestures, facial expressions, body language and tone of voice.
Formal language suits officials and people we don't know well: full sentences, polite requests, no slang. Informal language suits friends and family and may use contractions like I'm and can't.
A formal letter has: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation (Sir/Madam), body, complimentary close (Yours faithfully), and signature with name.
In India, the six-digit PIN code (Postal Index Number) helps the postal service deliver letters to the right area.

example.q: Which line suits a leave application to the principal? (a) 'Hey, can I skip school on Monday?' (b) 'I request you to kindly grant me leave for two days.'
steps: A principal is addressed formally, so slang like 'Hey' and 'skip' is not suitable.
Line (b) is a polite, complete request using formal words like 'request' and 'kindly grant'.
example.answer: Line (b), because it is formal and polite.

learn.reallife: Writing a leave application, sending a festival message to your cousin and giving directions to a visitor all need different styles of communication.

games.title: Parts of a formal letter
games.prompt: Put the parts of a formal letter in order, from top to bottom

quiz.q: Which of these is non-verbal communication?
quiz.explain: A namaste is a gesture; it communicates without words.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only written or spoken words count as communication

quiz.q: Which sentence is most suitable for a letter to a municipal officer?
options: I wish to draw your attention to the broken street lights in our colony.
Hey, the lights are kaput again.
quiz.explain: Formal letters use complete, polite sentences without slang.
quiz.mistake: Uses chatty, informal language in a formal letter

quiz.q: Which salutation is used in a formal letter to a principal?
quiz.explain: 'Sir' or 'Madam' (or 'Respected Sir/Madam') is the formal salutation.
quiz.mistake: Uses an informal greeting in a formal letter

quiz.q: Which closing is used in a formal letter that begins with 'Sir'?
quiz.explain: A formal letter beginning 'Sir/Madam' traditionally ends with 'Yours faithfully'.
quiz.mistake: Uses a friendly letter ending in a formal letter

quiz.q: What does PIN stand for in 'PIN code'?
quiz.explain: PIN stands for Postal Index Number, the six-digit code used by India Post.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with a bank PIN

quiz.q: What is 'body language'?
options: A language spoken in one region
Communication through posture, gestures and expressions
quiz.explain: Body language is how our posture, gestures and expressions send messages.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'language' must always mean words

quiz.q: Read: 'Dadaji in the village cannot hear well on the phone, so Mitali writes him a postcard every month in big, clear letters. He keeps them all in a tin box and reads them aloud to visitors.' Why does Mitali write postcards?
options: Because Dadaji cannot hear well on the phone
Because postcards are cheaper than sweets
Because her teacher told her to
quiz.explain: The passage says he cannot hear well on the phone, so she chose writing.
quiz.mistake: Picks a reason not given in the passage

quiz.q: Which of these is a feature of informal writing?
quiz.explain: Contractions are common in friendly, informal writing; the others belong to formal letters.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the features of formal and informal letters

teach.ask: Gappu holds up a leaf-letter: "I want to write to the Forest Officer about our cut-down tree. Can I start with 'Hey buddy'?"
teach.praise: Tweet! A formal letter: address, date, subject, 'Sir', polite words and 'Yours faithfully'. The Forest Officer will listen!
teach.nudge: Hmm, is a Forest Officer a friend? What kind of language and greeting should I use?

topics.title: The power of words: shades of meaning

learn.hook: 'Slim' or 'skinny'? 'Curious' or 'nosy'? One small word choice can make someone smile or frown!
points: Words can hurt or heal, so we choose them with care. 'Think before you speak' is good advice.
Denotation is a word's dictionary meaning. Connotation is the feeling a word carries: 'thrifty' sounds positive, 'stingy' sounds negative, though both describe careful spending.
Polite words and phrases (please, could you, thank you, I'm sorry) make requests and disagreements kinder.
Tricky homophones: its (belonging to it) / it's (it is); your (belonging to you) / you're (you are); their (belonging to them) / there (a place) / they're (they are).
The saying 'The pen is mightier than the sword' means ideas and words can have more power than force.

example.q: Which feedback on a friend's drawing is kinder and more useful? (a) 'Your drawing is bad.' (b) 'I love the colours; maybe the trees could be a little bigger?'
steps: (a) only judges and gives no help.
(b) praises something real and gives a gentle, specific suggestion.
example.answer: (b), because it is kind and gives a clear suggestion for improvement.

learn.reallife: Saying 'Could you please pass the chutney?' instead of 'Give the chutney!' at the dinner table is the power of words in action.

quiz.q: What is the connotation of a word?
options: The feeling or idea it suggests beyond its basic meaning
quiz.explain: Connotation is the emotional shade a word carries, positive or negative.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up connotation with denotation

quiz.q: Which word describes someone careful with money in a positive way?
quiz.explain: 'Thrifty' praises careful spending; the others suggest meanness.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the negative shade of the other words

quiz.q: Your friend's speech was too long. Which response is the kindest and most useful?
options: Your opening was great; a shorter middle part would make it even better.
quiz.explain: It praises a real strength and gives a gentle, specific suggestion.
quiz.mistake: Thinks honesty has to be harsh

quiz.q: Choose the correct word: '___ raining, so take an umbrella.'
quiz.explain: 'It's' is short for 'it is': It is raining.
quiz.mistake: Uses the possessive 'its' instead of 'it is'

quiz.q: What is the denotation of a word?
quiz.explain: Denotation is the literal, dictionary meaning.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up denotation with connotation

quiz.q: What does 'The pen is mightier than the sword' mean?
options: Words and ideas can be more powerful than force
quiz.explain: The saying means ideas and words can change the world more than violence can.
quiz.mistake: Reads the saying literally

quiz.q: Read: 'When Arnav forgot his lines on stage, a boy in the front row giggled. But his teacher whispered, "Take a breath; you know this." Arnav finished his speech and later said those words carried him through.' What does this show?
options: Teachers should not speak during events
Encouraging words can give a person strength
quiz.explain: The teacher's few kind words helped Arnav finish, showing the power of encouragement.
quiz.mistake: Focuses on a minor detail instead of the main point

quiz.q: Which word has a negative connotation?
quiz.explain: 'Nosy' suggests poking into others' business; the others sound positive or neutral.
quiz.mistake: Does not sense the negative shade in 'nosy'

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "If 'slim' and 'skinny' mean nearly the same, why does my friend get upset when I say 'skinny'?"
teach.praise: Chirp! Words carry feelings called connotations. I'll choose kind words from now on!
teach.nudge: Hmm, the dictionary meaning is close, so what else does a word carry with it?

topics.title: Words: a poem about words, and parts of speech

learn.hook: A single word can be a noun at breakfast and a verb by lunch. Words are shape-shifters!
points: The poem 'Words' in this lesson is about the power of words.
Metaphors help poets show the power of words: words as seeds, thorns or wings.
English has eight parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and interjection.
The same word can be a different part of speech in different sentences: 'Switch on the light' (noun), 'Light the diya' (verb), 'a light bag' (adjective).
Conjunctions (and, but, because) join words or clauses; prepositions (in, on, under) show how a noun relates to other words; interjections (Wow! Oh!) express sudden feeling.

example.q:
Read this original poem:
'Words are seeds we gently sow,
In other hearts they root and grow;
A harsh word is a thorn that stings,
A kind word gives the spirit wings.
So weigh each word before it flies:
Once spoken, no word ever dies.'
What is the poem's message, and name one metaphor.
steps: Lines 1 to 4 show words growing in hearts, stinging or lifting people.
Lines 5 and 6 advise us to think before we speak because words last.
'Words are seeds' says words ARE seeds, without 'like' or 'as'.
example.answer: Message: words have lasting power, so think before you speak. Metaphor: 'Words are seeds' (also 'A harsh word is a thorn').

learn.reallife: A kind message to a friend before an exam can stay with them for years; so can a mean comment. That's why we weigh our words.

games.title: Words and the poem
items: In the original poem, words are compared to seeds.
The first line says 'Words are seeds we gently sow'.
'A kind word gives the spirit wings' means kind words lift a person's mood.
Wings suggest feeling light and hopeful.
A word can belong to only one part of speech.
'Light' can be a noun, a verb or an adjective, depending on the sentence.
In 'She will light the diya', 'light' is a verb.
It names the action she will do.
An interjection expresses a sudden feeling, like 'Oh!' or 'Hurray!'
Conjunctions join clauses; prepositions link a noun or pronoun to other words.

quiz.q: 'Words are seeds we gently sow.' Which device is used?
quiz.explain: Words are said to BE seeds, without 'like' or 'as', so it is a metaphor.
quiz.mistake: Calls every comparison a simile

quiz.q: What does 'A harsh word is a thorn that stings' mean?
options: Harsh words are hard to spell
quiz.explain: Like a thorn, a harsh word causes pain.
quiz.mistake: Takes the metaphor literally

quiz.q: What is the main message of the original poem 'Words are seeds we gently sow...'?
options: Think carefully before you speak, because words last
quiz.explain: The poem says words grow in hearts and never die, so we must weigh them.
quiz.mistake: Picks a literal idea about seeds

quiz.q: In 'The light in the kitchen is on', what part of speech is 'light'?
quiz.explain: 'The light' names a thing, so it is a noun here.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a word always has the same part of speech

quiz.q: In 'She carried a light bag', what part of speech is 'light'?
quiz.explain: 'Light' describes the bag, so it is an adjective.
quiz.mistake: Does not check what the word is doing in the sentence

quiz.q: Which word is the conjunction in 'I wanted to call, but my phone had no charge'?
quiz.explain: 'But' joins the two clauses and shows contrast.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a conjunction with a verb or noun

quiz.q: Which word is an adverb in 'He spoke softly to the baby'?
quiz.explain: 'Softly' tells how he spoke, so it is an adverb.
quiz.mistake: Picks the verb instead of the word describing it

quiz.q: What does 'weigh each word' mean in the poem?
options: Think carefully about what you say
quiz.explain: To weigh words is to consider them carefully before speaking.
quiz.mistake: Reads 'weigh' literally

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: "Are words really that powerful? They're just sounds!"
teach.praise: Chirp! Words can hurt or heal, so I must think before I speak. Words are seeds, not just sounds!
teach.nudge: But what can a word do to someone's feelings? And what should I do before I speak?
